title: Operating Systems and Concurrency
description: Processes, scheduling, synchronization, and system-call concepts.

questions.prompt: What is a process?
options: A running program together with its execution state and resources
questions.explanation: An operating system represents a process with an address space and execution context, among other resources.

questions.prompt: What do threads in one process commonly share?
options: The process address space and open resources
Their own separate copies of every global variable
questions.explanation: Threads share process resources while retaining their own execution stacks and register state.

questions.prompt: A context switch can add overhead because the processor must save and restore execution state.
questions.explanation: Switching tasks consumes time and can affect caches and translation structures.

questions.prompt: What is a system call?
options: A controlled request from a program to an operating-system service
A function call that always stays in user mode
questions.explanation: System calls provide an interface to privileged services such as file I/O and process management.

questions.prompt: Why do processors distinguish user and kernel modes?
options: Restrict privileged operations to trusted operating-system code
Make all applications run at equal privilege
Remove the need for memory protection
Ensure every process has one thread
questions.explanation: Privilege modes let the OS protect critical hardware and system state from ordinary application code.

questions.prompt: What does preemptive scheduling allow an operating system to do?
options: Interrupt a running task to schedule another
Make every task complete in one time slice
questions.explanation: The scheduler can reclaim the CPU, for example when a time slice expires or a higher-priority task becomes ready.

questions.prompt: Which goals can influence CPU scheduling policy?
options: Minimizing the number of source files
questions.explanation: Scheduling balances interactive response, useful work completed, and fair access among tasks.

questions.prompt: What is a race condition?
options: Behavior depends on the timing or interleaving of concurrent operations
A process uses too much disk
A program has a syntax error
questions.explanation: Unsynchronized access to shared state can produce results that vary with execution order.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a mutex?
options: Provide mutual exclusion around a critical section
questions.explanation: A mutex allows at most one owner into a protected region at a time.

questions.prompt: A deadlock requires a circular wait among processes or resources.
questions.explanation: Circular wait is one of the four Coffman conditions required for deadlock.

questions.prompt: Which are Coffman conditions associated with deadlock?
questions.explanation: Deadlock requires all four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

questions.prompt: What can a counting semaphore represent?
options: A count of available instances of a resource
questions.explanation: A counting semaphore tracks permits and coordinates access to a bounded number of resources.

questions.prompt: How should a thread typically use a condition variable?
options: Wait in a loop that checks a shared predicate under the associated lock
Assume a signal cannot be missed
Treat it as a persistent message queue
questions.explanation: Spurious wakeups and races are possible, so a waiter rechecks its condition while holding the lock.

questions.prompt: An atomic operation appears indivisible with respect to concurrent observers.
questions.explanation: Atomicity means other threads cannot observe a partially completed operation, though memory ordering may also matter.

questions.prompt: What is priority inversion?
options: A high-priority task waits on a resource held by a lower-priority task
A scheduler runs all tasks alphabetically
questions.explanation: A lower-priority lock holder can block a higher-priority task; priority inheritance can mitigate this.

questions.prompt: Why isolate process address spaces?
questions.explanation: Address-space isolation protects processes from accidental or unauthorized memory access by others.

questions.prompt: What can a Unix-like file descriptor refer to?
options: Only a directory name in source code
questions.explanation: File descriptors are process-local handles for open files and many other I/O objects, including pipes and sockets.

questions.prompt: What does copy-on-write defer?
options: Copying shared memory pages until a write occurs
Loading an executable until it exits
questions.explanation: Processes can initially share pages; a write triggers a private copy where needed.

questions.prompt: A user-space thread library can switch between threads without a kernel transition in some designs.
questions.explanation: User-level scheduling can perform context switches in user space, though blocking and multicore behavior depend on implementation.

questions.prompt: Why should asynchronous signal handlers be kept limited?
options: They may interrupt code at arbitrary points and allow only safe operations
They run only after the process exits
They are guaranteed to execute on a new process
questions.explanation: Handlers can interrupt inconsistent program state, so only async-signal-safe operations should be used.
